data.title: API DTO typing end to end
data.subtitle: Entity, boundaries, Omit leak, FE sync

cards.front: Entity vs create DTO vs response DTO — who owns what?
cards.meaning: Entity owns DB / domain and often holds secrets like passwordHash. Create/update DTOs are inbound HTTP shapes: passwords in plain for input only, never hashes outbound. Response DTOs are outbound HTTP projections with no secrets.

cards.front: What is the canonical field list, and what are DTOs?
cards.meaning: The entity is the canonical field list. Request and response types are projections for directions of travel — inbound vs outbound — not a second copy of the whole domain object. One mega-type for entity + create + update + response conflates secrets and PATCH optionality.

cards.front: Do @Body() types parse or validate JSON?
cards.meaning: No. Untrusted JSON enters as a plain object. Types on @Body() erase — they do not parse or validate.

cards.front: Where should you validate, and why once?
cards.meaning: Validate/parse once at the HTTP boundary. Inner service code trusts the DTO type because the edge already enforced it. Nest: class-validator plus ValidationPipe on DTO classes. Elsewhere: zod / yup / Valibot — parse → typed value or error. UI checks and TS annotations do not replace this.
The schema is the runtime source of truth; the inferred type stays in sync with parse rules. CreateUser.parse(req.body) throws or returns validated data.
cards.example: type CreateUser = z.infer<typeof CreateUser>; const dto = CreateUser.parse(req.body);

cards.front: Response typed Omit<User,'passwordHash'> but hash still in JSON — how?
cards.meaning: Types erase. Omit only changes what the compiler thinks. If the real object still has passwordHash, JSON.stringify includes it. Fix: map to a new object/DTO with only public fields — never return user as UserResponseDto as the only defense. In Nest, add @Exclude() plus ClassSerializerInterceptor.
cards.example: function toPublic(user: User): Omit<User, 'passwordHash'> { return user; } // JSON may still include passwordHash

cards.meaning: Hash the password, save the User entity, then return a plain object with only public fields. The entity must not leave the service as the HTTP payload — returning entities “because the return type omits secrets” is the leak.
cards.example: return { id: user.id, name: user.name, email: user.email, createdAt: user.createdAt };

cards.front: What is the end-to-end DTO flow both directions?
cards.meaning: Client JSON → validate CreateUserDto (pipe / zod) → service hashes password and saves User → map to UserResponseDto (no passwordHash) → optional ClassSerializerInterceptor → JSON response. On the client: treat fetch JSON as unknown and parse into UI types.

cards.front: Are both inbound and outbound API edges boundaries?
cards.meaning: Yes. Inbound validation and outbound stripping/mapping on the server; the frontend should not blindly trust network JSON either.

cards.front: What are Nest’s inbound vs outbound DTO layers?
cards.meaning: Inbound: class-validator DTO classes plus ValidationPipe (transform, whitelist). Outbound: explicit response mapping and/or @Exclude plus ClassSerializerInterceptor. Compile-time Omit is not a security control. Forget whitelist and extra body keys can reach persistence.

cards.front: How do you keep FE and BE API types in sync?
cards.meaning: One of: a shared types package both sides import; OpenAPI/Swagger codegen of a TS client; or GraphQL codegen of operations/hooks. Hand-copied User interfaces drift (renames, Date vs ISO string). Shared TypeScript types still do not validate runtime JSON — pair with zod or a generated decoder.

cards.front: Why is (await res.json()) as UserResponseDto unsafe?
cards.meaning: The assertion lies — there is no check that JSON matches. A backend bug or proxy can add fields. Types erase on both sides.
cards.example: const data = (await res.json()) as UserResponseDto; setUser(data); // trap

cards.front: What is the safer frontend pattern for API JSON?
cards.meaning: Treat the payload as unknown, then schema-parse (e.g. UserResponseSchema.parse) to a typed value. Same boundary idea as Nest pipes.

cards.front: What happens if you forget ValidationPipe whitelist?
cards.meaning: Extra body keys can reach persistence if not stripped. whitelist removes properties without decorator metadata — part of inbound boundary hardening.

cards.front: Why not one type for entity + create + update + response?
cards.meaning: Anti-pattern: secrets and optional PATCH fields get conflated. Derive projections from a canonical entity or schema instead.
